annotation_note: Captions describe visually inspected figures and their surrounding section context. Groups preserve related views; a comparison figure contains multiple views within one image. Example screenshots demonstrate a specific principle, not complete implementation or accessibility conformance.

rules.title: Start with a feature, not a layout
rules.when: A new screen is stuck on navigation, page chrome or the app shell.
rules.summary: Design the smallest useful feature around its real data and actions before choosing the surrounding shell.
rules.caution: Reuse established navigation in an existing product; this advice targets an undecided new design.

figures.caption: Three competing page shells leave navigation and layout undecided before a feature exists.
A flight-search form focuses on departure, destination, dates and the search action.
The flight-search feature gains typography, icons and a split background while remaining the focal point.

rules.title: Detail comes later
rules.when: Colors, fonts and shadows are slowing early layout decisions.
rules.summary: Explore structure in low fidelity or grayscale, then add detail once the hierarchy works.
rules.caution: Grayscale is a design exercise, not a demand to remove a product's established visual language.

figures.caption: A thick-marker sketch captures form and plan-card layout without detailed styling.
A grayscale storage-plan checkout establishes hierarchy through spacing, weight and contrast.
Purple accents enhance the same checkout after its grayscale hierarchy is established.

rules.title: Don’t design too much
rules.when: Mockups imply features or edge cases that are outside the current delivery scope.
rules.summary: Design and implement one useful slice, learning from the working interface before expanding.
rules.caution: Keep required functionality and known constraints; simplify only genuinely optional scope.

figures.caption: A collage of many application screens illustrates the complexity of designing everything at once.
One screen is isolated from the surrounding screens to focus work on the next feature.
A circular Design and Code loop illustrates alternating design with implementation.
A comment form includes attachment controls that expand the implementation scope.
The comment form omits attachments and retains the message field and posting action.

rules.title: Choose a personality
rules.when: The interface feels generic or its typography, colors, corners and copy disagree.
rules.summary: Choose a coherent visual and verbal personality suited to the audience.
rules.caution: Preserve an existing brand; color associations and example fonts are possibilities, not universal meanings.

figures.caption: Banking photography and a community illustration give two landing pages different personalities.
A bookkeeping hero uses a serif headline to convey a classic professional tone.
An icon-library hero uses a rounded sans-serif and pill button for a playful tone.
A workspace hero uses a neutral sans-serif over photography.
A chat-product hero uses blue accents on its action and chat preview.
A rooftop-lounge hero combines gold accents with monochrome city photography.
A city-tour hero uses a pink action beside a bright illustrated skyline.
A meeting-room hero uses modestly rounded controls in a restrained layout.
A startup-dashboard hero uses rounded cards and pill actions for a softer feel.
An investment hero uses square action buttons and a rectangular photo for a formal feel.
An identity-verification form addresses the user formally on a dark blue background.
An identity-verification form uses conversational copy and pink accents for a friendly tone.

rules.title: Limit your choices
rules.when: Every component introduces another slightly different size, shade or shadow.
rules.summary: Constrain choices to a reusable scale and compare neighboring options in context.
rules.caution: Use the project's existing tokens before proposing new scales.

figures.caption: Three nearly identical blue buttons illustrate unproductive decisions between arbitrary color values.
Ten predefined blue shades constrain later color choices.
A short list of named pixel sizes constrains typography choices.
Four squares compare 12, 16, 24 and 32 pixel sizes.
Three Bookmark buttons compare icons at 12, 16 and 24 pixels in context.
The next comparison shifts to 16, 24 and 32 pixel icons, fading the rejected smaller option.

rules.title: Not all elements are equal
rules.when: A crowded dashboard gives all information and actions equal emphasis.
rules.summary: Identify the primary content and soften secondary information before adding decoration.
rules.caution: Density can be intentional; preserve information needed for the user's task.

figures.caption: An investment dashboard gives headings, balances, labels and colored row actions similar visual priority.
The dashboard emphasizes balance values, softens labels and navigation, and quiets repeated Buy and Sell actions.

rules.title: Size isn’t everything
rules.when: The main text is oversized while supporting details are too small.
rules.summary: Use weight and color alongside size to establish readable levels of emphasis.
rules.caution: Secondary text still needs readable contrast and size; example pixel values are not mandates.

figures.caption: A tour card relies on large size differences, leaving supporting details small and the title oversized.
A smaller bold title and bold price establish emphasis with font weight.
Larger supporting copy uses softer colors to remain secondary without becoming tiny.
The tour card combines two weights and three text colors into a readable hierarchy.

rules.title: Don’t use grey text on colored backgrounds
rules.when: Secondary text on a colored panel looks grey, washed out or disabled.
rules.summary: Choose an opaque related text color and check it against the actual background.
rules.caution: Measure contrast; transparency is acceptable when its composited result is deliberate and verified.

figures.caption: Neutral grey secondary text looks disconnected from a teal testimonial footer.
A grayscale ramp explains foreground and background contrast on a neutral testimonial footer.
Semi-transparent white secondary text looks muted on a teal footer.
A magnified patterned footer shows background lines bleeding through translucent letters.
Opaque light teal secondary text harmonizes with the footer and stays solid over its pattern.

rules.title: Emphasize by de-emphasizing
rules.when: The active navigation or main content cannot stand out because neighboring elements compete.
rules.summary: Reduce the emphasis of competitors, such as inactive links or a sidebar panel.
rules.caution: Inactive navigation is still available navigation, not a disabled control; maintain contrast and a non-color active cue.

figures.caption: Dark inactive navigation items compete with the purple active Orders item.
Softer inactive navigation text makes the unchanged purple Orders item stand out.
Removing the itinerary sidebar's white panel lets the main booking form take priority.

rules.title: Labels are a last resort
rules.when: Displayed data is buried in repetitive label-value pairs.
rules.summary: Use recognizable formats or combine labels with values, emphasizing what people scan for.
rules.caution: This rule concerns displayed data, not form labels or accessible names. Keep labels when meaning is ambiguous or users scan by label.

figures.caption: Repeated Name, Job Title, Email and Phone labels flatten a contact card's hierarchy.
A contact card uses recognizable formats and context, emphasizing the name and role.
A product card replaces In stock: 12 with 12 left in stock, emphasizing the quantity.
A property card folds bedroom and bathroom labels into values with supporting icons.
A heart-rate card emphasizes 82 BPM while treating the Heart rate label as supporting text.
A technical specification table emphasizes Height, Width and Depth because readers scan by label.

rules.title: Separate visual hierarchy from document hierarchy
rules.when: A large page title competes with more important task content.
rules.summary: Choose heading elements for document structure and style their visual emphasis independently.
rules.caution: Do not change heading levels or remove accessible structure merely to make text smaller.

figures.caption: A large Manage Account page heading competes with the settings content.
A smaller Manage Account heading labels the page while giving its content more emphasis.

rules.title: Balance weight and contrast
rules.when: Solid icons overpower nearby labels, or thin borders are either harsh or invisible.
rules.summary: Balance visual area against contrast: soften heavy icons or slightly thicken pale separators.
rules.caution: Required control boundaries and meaningful icons need adequate contrast; decorative examples are not universal tokens.

figures.caption: Filled and thin letterforms cover different surface areas, explaining why weight attracts attention.
Dark solid sidebar icons overpower the adjacent labels in a music app.
Lighter icons balance their visual weight against darker text labels.
Two feeds show a thin divider that is either too dark or too faint.
A thicker, lighter divider separates feed items without a harsh dark line.

rules.title: Semantics are secondary
rules.when: Every action is a loud colored button, including rare destructive actions.
rules.summary: Assign primary, secondary and tertiary emphasis according to each action's role in the current task.
rules.caution: The title refers to visual button priority, not HTML semantics. Keep destructive labels and required confirmations clear.

figures.caption: Delete, Edit and Publish buttons all use strong fills and compete on a listing card.
Publish is filled, Edit is softly tinted, and Delete becomes a quiet tertiary action.
Filled, outlined and text treatments demonstrate primary, secondary and tertiary actions on varied backgrounds.
The same Unpublish action receives primary, secondary or tertiary emphasis according to its role.
A deactivation dialog makes the destructive action red and primary at the confirmation step.

rules.title: Start with too much white space
rules.when: A card or form feels cramped and every section barely fits.
rules.summary: Start with generous spacing, then remove excess until grouping and density fit the task.
rules.caution: Dense dashboards are valid when deliberate; whitespace must not hide essential information.

figures.caption: A two-factor setup form gains space around its title, instructions, field group and action.
A cramped ratings card is compared with a roomier version while exploring spacing.
A ratings card trims excessive gaps while retaining clear separation between sections.
A sports dashboard keeps statistics and a roster compact for simultaneous scanning.

rules.title: Establish a spacing and sizing system
rules.when: Margins and padding vary arbitrarily across similar components.
rules.summary: Replace arbitrary values with a spacing scale whose steps remain perceptibly different.
rules.caution: Reuse existing tokens; the scale and percentage guidance here are starting points, not required replacements.

figures.caption: A hotel card uses many unrelated gaps such as 13, 15, 21, 25 and 26 pixels.
Download buttons compare 16, 20 and 24 pixel icons to show perceptible relative size changes.
Delivery cards at 500 and 520 pixels look nearly alike despite a 20 pixel change.
A spacing scale runs from 4 to 768 pixels with wider steps at larger sizes.
The hotel card replaces arbitrary gaps with consistent 12 and 24 pixel spacing.

rules.title: You don’t have to fill the whole screen
rules.when: Forms or content stretch across a wide viewport without gaining usefulness.
rules.summary: Constrain content to a readable width; put supporting descriptions beside fields when useful.
rules.caution: Wide tables and other content may legitimately need the available width; reflow at narrow sizes.

figures.caption: A cart stretches across the browser, separating product details from prices unnecessarily.
A constrained cart keeps descriptions, prices and totals close enough to scan.
A narrow login card sits beneath full-width navigation.
A podcast screen arranges artwork, playback and episodes in a narrow mobile layout.
The desktop podcast screen keeps its content compact while widening the surrounding background.
A settings page stacks section descriptions and fields into a long narrow column.
Settings descriptions move beside their fields, using desktop width without stretching the inputs.

rules.title: Grids are overrated
rules.when: A percentage sidebar or grid-bound card becomes too wide or too narrow at different viewports.
rules.summary: Size stable elements for their content and let the main content flex within useful limits.
rules.caution: This critiques rigid percentage layouts, not CSS Grid. Collapse or reflow sidebars when narrow space demands it.

figures.caption: A page shell is overlaid with a twelve-column layout grid.
Three, six and three grid columns become 25, 50 and 25 percent widths.
A sidebar occupies 25 percent of a medium-width shell.
The same percentage sidebar wastes space as the browser widens.
The same percentage sidebar becomes cramped as the browser narrows.
An invoice dashboard keeps its sidebar width steady while its main cards reflow.
A feed card preserves avatar size while the text column changes width.
A login card is assigned a fraction of a column grid.
Changing the login card's column span changes its width at another layout size.
Breakpoint-dependent column spans make a login card wider in the smaller browser.
A maximum-width login card keeps its useful size, shrinking only on a narrow viewport.

rules.title: Relative sizing doesn’t scale
rules.when: Mobile headings dominate the screen, or button variants look like zoomed copies.
rules.summary: Tune headline sizes and component padding independently across size variants.
rules.caution: Keep body text readable and hit targets usable; shrinking every dimension is not the goal.

figures.caption: A desktop article uses a large heading relative to body copy.
Keeping the desktop heading-to-body ratio makes the mobile heading wrap excessively.
The mobile heading shrinks independently, keeping more body content visible.
A base button shows its font size and horizontal and vertical padding.
Button sizes scale padding proportionally with font size and look like zoomed copies.
Large buttons receive more generous padding while small variants use tighter padding.

rules.title: Avoid ambiguous spacing
rules.when: Labels, headings, list items or horizontal controls appear connected to the wrong neighbors.
rules.summary: Make spacing inside a group smaller than spacing between groups.
rules.caution: Keep programmatic relationships such as label-to-input associations as well as visual grouping.

figures.caption: Restaurant results use dividers to make each group of details unambiguous.
Equal gaps above and below field labels obscure which input each label belongs to.
Labels sit closer to their inputs than to preceding fields, clarifying form groups.
More space above an article heading and less below connects it to the following paragraph.
Larger gaps between bullets distinguish list items from wrapped lines within each item.
Reaction counts move closer to their icons, with larger gaps between reaction groups.

rules.title: Establish a type scale
rules.when: Similar text roles use many nearly identical font sizes.
rules.summary: Define a small set of useful type sizes and reuse them by role.
rules.caution: Prefer existing tokens and avoid accidental em compounding; intentional relative sizing and fractional values are valid.

figures.caption: A product page accumulates many unrelated text sizes across its labels, price and delivery form.
A ratio-based type scale produces fractional values and large gaps between useful interface sizes.
A hand-picked scale ranges from 12 to 72 pixels with smaller steps for body sizes.
The product page reuses a small set of sizes for labels, body copy, title and price.
A type-size list expressed in em illustrates values whose computed size depends on the parent.

rules.title: Use good fonts
rules.when: Body text is hard to read or font selection is consuming the design process.
rules.summary: Start with a legible family and verify its actual weights, proportions and language coverage.
rules.caution: Popularity and number of styles are selection shortcuts, not quality guarantees; variable fonts need not have many files.

figures.caption: A grid of font families shows how many typeface choices are available.
A font directory filters sans-serif families by the number of available styles.
Futura and Proxima Nova compare tight spacing and shorter x-height with wider spacing and taller lowercase letters.
A font directory sorts families by popularity to narrow the choices.
Browser styles reveal the font family used in an existing delivery card.

rules.title: Keep your line length in check
rules.when: Paragraphs span too much of the page and are tiring to read.
rules.summary: Constrain reading measure independently of the wider layout.
rules.caution: The 45-75 character range is a prose heuristic; judge the actual script, font, device and content.

figures.caption: A paragraph stretches to about 120 characters per line.
A narrow paragraph demonstrates roughly 45 to 55 characters per line.
Two paragraphs compare roughly 55 to 65 and 65 to 75 characters per line.
Introductory text spans the full width of a three-column feature section.
A narrower introductory paragraph remains centered above the wider feature grid.

rules.title: Baseline, not center
rules.when: A title and smaller adjacent actions look vertically misaligned.
rules.summary: Align mixed text sizes on their baseline.
rules.caution: Use optical or center alignment when it suits icons or non-text controls; inspect the rendered result.

figures.caption: A card heading and smaller actions are vertically centered, leaving their text baselines uneven.
Moving the actions beside the larger heading exposes the mismatch caused by vertical centering.
The word typography marks the common baseline beneath its letterforms.
Baseline alignment places the heading and smaller actions on a shared reading line.

rules.title: Line-height is proportional
rules.when: Body lines are hard to track, or a wrapped heading feels disconnected.
rules.summary: Adjust line-height to both line length and font size, usually giving small or wide body text more room.
rules.caution: Test actual glyphs and wrapping; tight headline leading must not clip accents or overlap lines.

figures.caption: A magnified paragraph relates 16 pixel text to a 24 pixel line-height.
Tight line-height in a long paragraph makes it hard to find the next line after wrapping.
A narrow paragraph uses less line-height than a wider paragraph.
Increasing line-height opens dense small body copy and makes lines easier to follow.
Reducing headline line-height groups its large wrapped lines into a coherent heading.

rules.title: Not every link needs a color
rules.when: Repeated colored links overwhelm cards or navigation.
rules.summary: Establish hierarchy with weight and neutral tones where the component context already indicates interaction.
rules.caution: Keep links identifiable without hover, preserve keyboard focus, and distinguish inline prose links from surrounding text.

figures.caption: Links in an article paragraph use underlines and color to distinguish them from surrounding prose.
Blue titles and author links compete across a row of video cards.
Neutral bold titles establish hierarchy in the link-heavy video grid.
A secondary author link gains an underline on hover while the card titles retain emphasis.

rules.title: Align with readability in mind
rules.when: Long centered text or uneven numeric columns are hard to scan.
rules.summary: Align prose with its reading direction and numeric columns for comparison; keep centered text brief.
rules.caution: Account for RTL and locale-specific number formats. Justification needs careful hyphenation and language support.

figures.caption: A feed item aligns its name, role and paragraph to a shared left edge.
Short descriptions sit centered beneath feature icons and headings.
A long centered feature paragraph becomes easier to scan when left-aligned.
Shortening a long feature description makes the centered row more balanced.
Right-aligned stock prices and changes make magnitudes easier to compare down table columns.
Justified text without hyphenation produces large irregular spaces between words.
Hyphenation reduces the large gaps in the justified paragraph.

rules.title: Use letter-spacing effectively
rules.when: Headlines feel loose or all-caps labels feel crowded.
rules.summary: Keep body tracking near the typeface default, testing tighter headlines or wider uppercase text when useful.
rules.caution: Tracking adjustments are font- and script-dependent; do not apply Latin uppercase habits universally.

figures.caption: The same paragraph compares tight, normal and wide letter-spacing.
Open Sans and Oswald show different spacing and proportions in the same headline.
Slightly tighter tracking makes a large Open Sans headline more compact.
A typography diagram marks ascenders, x-height, baseline and descenders.
Wider letter-spacing improves separation in an all-caps role label.

rules.title: Ditch hex for HSL
rules.when: Related colors are difficult to reason about when editing raw color values.
rules.summary: Use a color model that exposes useful relationships and retain the project's palette format.
rules.caution: HSL explains the examples; it is not mandatory. Preserve an existing OKLCH or other color workflow.

figures.caption: A task donut chart labels three related blue shades with opaque hexadecimal values.
The same chart labels its shades with HSL values, exposing their shared hue and differing lightness.
An HSL hue wheel labels the angles of red, yellow, green, cyan, blue and magenta.
A blue ramp varies saturation from grey to vivid while holding hue and lightness constant.
Blue and pink become the same grey when HSL saturation reaches zero at equal lightness.
A blue ramp varies HSL lightness from black through vivid blue to white.
HSB and HSL color-picker planes place a vivid blue at different vertical positions.

rules.title: You need more colors than you think
rules.when: A small palette cannot support readable text, surfaces and semantic states.
rules.summary: Provide tonal ranges for neutrals, brand colors and the accent roles the product actually needs.
rules.caution: Do not create unused palette families or overwhelm the interface with saturated colors.

figures.caption: A five-swatch palette has no tonal range for backgrounds, text and component states.
A chat interface restricted to saturated palette colors becomes loud and hard to read.
The chat interface adds neutrals and tonal shades for calmer surfaces, readable text and distinct states.
A settings form assigns different grey shades to primary text, supporting text, borders and surfaces.
A broad neutral ramp spans near-black through near-white.
A blue ramp supports a progress indicator, tooltip, icons and primary action.
A teal ramp supplies the subtle New badge in a navigation bar.
Red shades serve an icon, accent border and tinted destructive button in a deactivation dialog.
Yellow shades provide dark warning text, a pale background and a visible alert icon.
Green shades support a positive stock trend, sparkline and tinted change badge.

rules.title: Define your shades up front
rules.when: Components accumulate slightly different ad hoc lightened and darkened colors.
rules.summary: Choose useful dark, middle and light anchors, fill a stable shade scale, and name semantic roles.
rules.caution: Judge shades in real components and both supported themes; the displayed base shade is not a contrast guarantee.

figures.caption: Primary, neutral and accent families each contain multiple tonal shades.
Three action buttons compare candidate base shades from too dark to too light.
An alert exercises a palette's dark text and light background endpoints.
A nine-slot palette starts with dark 900, base 500 and light 100 anchors.
Intermediate 700 and 300 shades split the gaps between the initial anchors.
The remaining gaps are filled to complete a nine-step color palette.
A nine-step blue-grey ramp applies the same palette-building process to neutrals.

rules.title: Don’t let lightness kill your saturation
rules.when: Light and dark palette shades look washed out or muddy.
rules.summary: Adjust saturation or chroma and sometimes hue while shaping the tonal range.
rules.caution: The HSL brightness approximation shown in the examples is not WCAG relative luminance. HSL hue offsets do not transfer directly to OKLCH.

figures.caption: A blue palette keeps saturation constant across a range of HSL lightness values.
Raising saturation toward the light and dark endpoints keeps the blue palette more vivid.
Pure yellow appears much brighter than pure blue.
Yellow and blue have identical HSL saturation and lightness despite different perceived brightness.
The weighted RGB brightness approximation illustrates perceived brightness; it is not the WCAG contrast formula.
A hue-versus-brightness plot shows yellow and cyan peaks and a deep blue trough.
Three fully saturated blue swatches vary only in HSL lightness.
A blue play icon uses a pale-to-vivid gradient created by changing lightness.
A cyan-to-blue hue shift keeps the play icon's gradient vivid.
A yellow-to-orange hue shift creates a warm vivid gradient on a play icon.
Rotating darker yellow shades toward orange avoids the muddy olive appearance of lightness-only shades.
Light cyan attribution text sits on a dark blue testimonial panel.

rules.title: Greys don’t have to be grey
rules.when: Neutral surfaces feel disconnected from the intended warm or cool personality.
rules.summary: Use a coherent, subtly tinted neutral ramp when it serves the design.
rules.caution: Neutral greys and black are valid choices; preserve the existing brand and measure text contrast.

figures.caption: A zero-saturation ramp runs from black to white.
An invoice dashboard uses blue-tinted greys for text, panels and page background.
Neutral and blue-tinted grey ramps show how small amounts of saturation create a cooler palette.
A warm grey ramp uses yellow-orange hues with adjusted saturation across shades.

rules.title: Accessible doesn’t have to mean ugly
rules.when: Readable status colors become too visually heavy, or colored text loses its character.
rules.summary: Try dark colored text on a light tint, checking actual foreground-background contrast.
rules.caution: Normal text needs 4.5:1; large text needs 3:1 at 18pt/24px regular or 14pt/about 18.67px bold. Do not round a failing ratio up.

figures.caption: A table compares normal and large text examples with contrast ratios and AA or AAA grades.
White text on bright green, yellow and pink status badges is marked as failing contrast.
Darkening badge fills improves the displayed contrast ratios but makes statuses visually heavy.
Dark colored text on pale status fills provides strong contrast with quieter visual emphasis.
Very pale secondary text on a purple support panel meets the shown contrast target but loses much of its color.
Cyan secondary text retains color on the same purple panel while meeting the shown contrast target.

rules.title: Don’t rely on color alone
rules.when: Trends, statuses or chart categories are distinguishable only by hue.
rules.summary: Pair color with labels, signs, icons, patterns or another independent signal.
rules.caution: Lightness differences help but do not alone identify every chart series; preserve labels and values.

figures.caption: Revenue badges encode direction only with red and green, which converge in a color-vision simulation.
Up and down arrows make the revenue direction explicit in addition to color.
Donut-chart hues become difficult to distinguish in a blue-yellow color-vision simulation.
Different lightness levels keep the donut segments more distinct in the simulation.

rules.title: Emulate a light source
rules.when: Raised and inset controls feel flat or their light cues contradict each other.
rules.summary: Use a consistent implied light direction with restrained edge highlights and shadows.
rules.caution: Depth is optional and should suit the established visual style; avoid decorative cues that imply nonexistent controls.

figures.caption: Property filters combine raised selects with inset checkboxes and a recessed range track.
A blue paneled door shows highlights on raised top edges and shadows below.
A side profile shows overhead light hitting a raised top edge more strongly than its lower edge.
Recessed cabinet panels show shadows near the top and highlights at the bottom.
A recessed side profile shows the top lip blocking light and the lower edge receiving it.
A flat Create Account button is paired with the raised profile it should suggest.
A subtle light top edge makes the button read as raised.
A small shadow below the button completes its raised appearance.
A flat upload target is paired with the recessed profile it should suggest.
A lighter bottom edge begins to make the upload target look recessed.
An inset shadow at the top completes the upload target's recessed appearance.
Small highlights and shadows distinguish the input, checkbox and raised signup button in a dark form.

rules.title: Use shadows to convey elevation
rules.when: Buttons, menus and dialogs appear to sit at arbitrary or indistinguishable depths.
rules.summary: Choose shadows from a small elevation scale matched to each element's layering role.
rules.caution: Shadow does not fix stacking, clipping or focus behavior; dark themes may need other separation cues.

figures.caption: Front and side views relate stronger shadows to greater distance above an interface surface.
A small shadow gives a Publish button modest elevation.
A medium shadow separates an account dropdown from the page behind it.
A broad soft shadow lifts a password dialog above its underlying form.
Five shadow samples progress from close-to-surface to strongly elevated.
A lifted playlist row gains a shadow while being reordered.
A Subscribe button's shadow shrinks in its pressed state.

rules.title: Shadows can have two parts
rules.when: A shadow feels muddy or its surface edge lacks definition.
rules.summary: Combine a broad soft shadow with a tighter contact shadow, reducing the latter at higher elevation.
rules.caution: Use the project's elevation tokens and inspect both supported themes; two shadows are a technique, not a requirement.

figures.caption: An event card uses both a tight edge shadow and a broader soft shadow.
A notification and a plant pot illustrate the larger shadow cast by direct light.
The same notification and pot illustrate a tight contact shadow near the surface.
Separate direct and contact shadows are combined on a notification card.
A multi-level shadow scale reduces the contact component as elevation increases.

rules.title: Even flat designs can have depth
rules.when: A flat interface needs clearer separation without realistic soft shadows.
rules.summary: Use surface tones or a crisp offset shadow to indicate layering.
rules.caution: Lightness-to-depth is a visual convention, not a universal rule; verify it in the current theme.

figures.caption: A social feed separates white panels from a pale background without prominent soft shadows.
A white login panel reads closer than the darker supporting signup area.
Shopping-cart rows use a solid offset shadow with no blur to suggest depth.

rules.title: Overlap elements to create layers
rules.when: Separate blocks feel disconnected, or overlapping images visually collide.
rules.summary: Let selected elements cross a section boundary and use a background-colored gap between overlapping images.
rules.caution: Preserve readable content, focus visibility and narrow-screen flow; do not introduce overlap solely for decoration.

figures.caption: A flight-search card moves across the boundary between the hero image and page background.
A license-renewal card extends above and below its colored parent section.
Carousel arrows straddle the edges of a testimonial card.
A profile avatar overlaps a landscape cover without a separating edge and visually clashes with it.
A border matching the card background separates overlapping avatars from neighboring imagery.

rules.title: Use good photos
rules.when: Weak lighting or composition undermines an otherwise clear card or hero.
rules.summary: Use imagery with appropriate lighting, composition and subject matter at the actual display size.
rules.caution: Work with supplied assets and permissions; do not assume stock imagery suits every product or misrepresents it.

figures.caption: Better lighting and composition improve an apartment listing while its card layout stays the same.

rules.title: Text needs consistent contrast
rules.when: Hero text disappears over bright or dark parts of an image.
rules.summary: Treat the image or text backing to create a consistent readable foreground-background relationship.
rules.caution: Check the actual crop and every supported breakpoint; overlays and shadows do not automatically prove sufficient contrast.

figures.caption: A hero headline crosses both bright and dark areas of an untreated meeting-room photo.
White and dark text each disappear into different regions of the same busy photo.
A dark overlay makes light hero text more consistent across the photo.
Lower image contrast and higher brightness create a quieter backdrop for dark hero text.
A blue colorizing treatment gives light hero text a more uniform backdrop and ties the photo to the palette.
A broad blurred text shadow adds local separation around a light headline.

rules.title: Everything has an intended size
rules.when: Enlarged icons look chunky, small screenshots are unreadable, or favicons lose their shape.
rules.summary: Use graphics designed for the target size; crop, simplify or recapture screenshots as needed.
rules.caution: Keep real product details accurate; a small icon's visual size is separate from its interactive hit area.

figures.caption: Enlarging a raster logo makes its wordmark and play symbol visibly blurry.
Large feature icons look heavy beside their short text descriptions.
A small megaphone enlarged to 48 pixels looks chunky beside one drawn for that size.
Keeping the megaphone small inside a tinted circle fills space without enlarging the icon itself.
Feature icons remain small inside colored circles, balancing the adjacent text.
A full desktop task-app screenshot becomes unreadable when shrunk into a marketing section.
A capture of the smaller-device layout keeps task details legible in the same section.
A circular crop highlights one relevant area of the task app at a readable scale.
A simplified UI illustration substitutes lines for tiny text while preserving the product's shape.
A detailed starburst icon loses definition when reduced to favicon size.
A simplified starburst retains a recognizable silhouette at the small target size.

rules.title: Beware user-uploaded content
rules.when: Varied aspect ratios break card layouts, or avatars lose their visible edges.
rules.summary: Use consistent image containers with deliberate cropping and subtle edge treatment where needed.
rules.caution: Preserve the subject and meaningful content; cover-cropping is unsuitable when the entire image must be visible.

figures.caption: Different photo aspect ratios make recipe-card rows uneven.
Consistent image containers align the recipe cards into orderly rows.
A photo covers a fixed card container by cropping its overflow instead of distorting its proportions.
Light avatar backgrounds disappear into a white messaging interface.
A strong avatar border is compared with a subtler edge that interferes less with the photos.
A faint inset edge defines circular avatars against the surrounding white interface.

rules.title: Supercharge the defaults
rules.when: A sound layout feels generic because its existing elements receive no attention.
rules.summary: Refine list markers, quotation marks, link treatments and form-control styling.
rules.caution: Preserve semantics, keyboard interaction and visible states; use established accessible controls rather than rebuilding behavior for decoration.

figures.caption: Colored checkmark icons replace plain bullets in a feature list.
Padlock icons reinforce the meaning of a security-feature list.
Larger tinted quotation marks give a testimonial visual character.
A plain colored inline link gains emphasis through weight or a thicker underline.
Checkboxes and radio buttons gain a consistent purple treatment and clearer visual size.

rules.title: Add color with accent borders
rules.when: A restrained interface needs a small amount of identity or a clearer active state.
rules.summary: Add a purposeful accent line to a card, alert, heading or active navigation item.
rules.caution: Avoid redundant accents everywhere; selected-state cues must remain perceivable in supported display modes.

figures.caption: A slim cyan top border adds identity to a pricing card.
An underline adds a second cue to the active navigation item.
A blue side border strengthens the grouping of a tinted information alert.
A short colored bar adds a visual anchor beneath a section heading.
A narrow colored strip along the page top adds character to a restrained event landing page.

rules.title: Decorate your backgrounds
rules.when: Hierarchy and spacing work but a surface still feels plain.
rules.summary: Try a restrained background tone, gentle gradient or low-contrast decorative fragment.
rules.caution: Keep decoration behind the content and avoid degrading contrast or implying meaningful data.

figures.caption: A colored pricing panel gives an otherwise plain card a stronger identity.
Alternating colored, dark and pale backgrounds distinguish a landing page's sections.
A gentle blue gradient adds interest behind a feature grid.
A low-contrast contour pattern decorates an About me heading panel.
A restrained square pattern sits along a dark footer's lower edge.
A small dotted geometric fragment decorates the side of an article heading.
A low-contrast wave fragment adds detail beside a pricing heading.
A faint dotted world map sits behind a newsletter signup form.

rules.title: Don’t overlook empty states
rules.when: A first-use screen shows only absence and gives no clear next action.
rules.summary: Explain the feature and make its first useful action prominent, simplifying controls with no purpose yet.
rules.caution: Distinguish first use from filtered zero results and errors; keep filters visible when users need them to recover.

figures.caption: A contact list shows the populated state with search, previews and unread counts.
An empty contact screen offers only a No contacts found message and a small plus control.
An illustration, short explanation and prominent Add contact button guide the first action.
The first-use discounts screen removes irrelevant filters and tabs and focuses on creating a discount.

rules.title: Use fewer borders
rules.when: An interface looks boxed in by repeated outlines and dividers.
rules.summary: Use spacing, surface tones or a restrained shadow where they communicate the same grouping.
rules.caution: Retain required control boundaries, focus indicators and separators needed for dense data or forced-colors modes.

figures.caption: A contact picker outlines its container, search field and every row with borders.
A shadow replaces the contact picker's outer border.
Background fills separate the search and footer areas without extra outlines.
Row spacing and a selected-row tint replace most remaining dividers.

rules.title: Think outside the box
rules.when: A dropdown, table or choice group is hard to scan in its default presentation.
rules.summary: Reorganize related content with descriptions, grouped cells or selectable cards when it improves the task.
rules.caution: Preserve interaction semantics, keyboard behavior, data relationships and useful sorting; richer layouts need a narrow-screen plan.

figures.caption: A feature dropdown presents a long undifferentiated list of links.
The dropdown uses columns, icons, descriptions and a separate resources section to clarify choices.
A policy table gives related name, role, value and policy-type fields separate equal-weight columns.
Related values are stacked within cells to reduce columns and establish hierarchy.
Avatars and quiet status badges add scannable cues to the reorganized policy table.
A plan selector uses plain radio rows with capacities and prices in a single text line.
Selectable cards emphasize each plan's capacity and price and visibly mark the selected plan.

rules.title: Leveling up
rules.when: You want to understand which subtle decisions make an admired interface work.
rules.summary: Study unexpected choices and reconstruct a small example to expose details in spacing, type and layers.
rules.caution: Use reconstruction as a learning exercise when requested; apply principles to the current product's identity.

figures.caption: A dark date picker contrasts with the surrounding light interface.
A newsletter action sits inside the visual boundary of its email field.
A hero headline uses two text colors to emphasize part of the sentence.
An annotated card identifies tight headline leading, image cropping, layered shadows and uppercase tracking.
